clues: The edge of the land curves inward around my water.
I open out into a larger lake, sea, or ocean.
San Francisco has a famous example of me.
quest.example: San Francisco Bay curves into the land.

clues: I am a stretch of sand, shells, or small stones beside water.
Waves can move my sand or stones along the shore.
People often walk or play where my gently sloping land meets the water.
quest.example: A sandy Atlantic Ocean beach in Florida.

clues: I am a natural stream that is often small.
I may bubble over stones as I flow between banks.
People may also call me a creek or stream; these names can mean much the same thing.
quest.example: A little brook bubbles over pebbles.
quest.note: Brook, creek, and stream are overlapping names. The same waterway may have more than one name.

clues: I am a piece of coastal land that sticks out into the water.
I can point into a lake, sea, or ocean.
Cape Cod is a famous example. People may also call this kind of land a headland.
quest.example: Cape Cod reaches out into the Atlantic Ocean.
quest.note: Cape and headland can describe the same piece of coastal land.

clues: I am the area where land meets an ocean or sea.
I may have beaches, cliffs, or places where rivers meet the sea.
I am much like a shore, but my name usually means land beside the sea.
quest.example: Florida's Atlantic coast is next to the ocean.
quest.note: Coast usually means land beside the sea. Shore can also mean land beside a lake or river.

clues: I am a small area of water tucked into the coast.
Nearby land can shelter my water from large waves.
I am a small, protected bay, not a piece of land surrounded by water.
quest.example: A small sheltered cove might hold tiny boats.

clues: I am a natural flow of water, often smaller than a river.
I wind through land between two banks.
Some people would also call me a brook or stream. The names overlap.
quest.example: A creek winds past trees and rocks.
quest.note: Creek, brook, and stream are overlapping names. There is no worldwide size cutoff.

clues: I am water moving in a steady direction.
I can carry a floating leaf or boat along.
I can flow in rivers, lakes, and oceans.
quest.example: An ocean current carries water along the coast.

clues: I can grow where a river meets a lake or sea.
When the river slows, it may drop sand and mud that build up over time.
Not every river makes me, and I do not always look like a triangle.
quest.example: The Mississippi River makes a delta near the Gulf.

clues: I am the direction the water in a river is flowing.
A leaf floating with the river moves my way.
I lead toward where the river ends, not toward where it begins.
quest.example: A floating leaf goes downstream with the current.

clues: I am part of a sea or ocean with land around some of my sides.
The Gulf of Mexico is an example.
My name is similar to bay. There is no exact size rule separating bays and gulfs.
quest.example: The Gulf of Mexico is partly surrounded by land.
quest.note: A bay and a gulf can look alike. There is no exact size rule for their names.

clues: I am a sheltered place in the water where boats can stay.
Land or built walls may protect boats from rough waves.
A pier might be built inside me, but I am the protected water area.
quest.example: New York Harbor provides sheltered water for ships.

clues: I am land with water on every side.
You cannot walk to a larger piece of land without crossing water.
Madagascar and the islands of Hawaii are examples.
quest.example: Hawaii has many islands surrounded by ocean.

clues: I am a narrow strip of land joining two larger areas of land.
There is water on each side of my narrow strip.
Panama has a famous example. I am land, not a narrow water passage.
quest.example: The Isthmus of Panama links two larger land areas.
quest.note: An isthmus is land between bodies of water. A strait is water between areas of land.

clues: I am a body of water surrounded by land.
Rivers and streams may flow into or out of me.
I am often bigger than what people call a pond, but there is no worldwide size rule.
quest.example: Lake Michigan is a very large lake.
quest.note: Lakes are often larger than ponds, but there is no exact worldwide size rule.

clues: I am part of Earth's huge connected body of salty water.
The Pacific is the largest one with my name.
Together, my waters cover most of our planet.
quest.example: The Pacific Ocean covers a huge part of Earth.

clues: Water is on most sides of me, but I am still joined to other land.
Unlike an island, you can reach me by staying on land.
Florida is a familiar example of my shape.
quest.example: Florida sticks out into the Atlantic and Gulf waters.

clues: I am a body of still water surrounded by land.
I am often small or shallow, with ducks or water plants.
People sometimes call a similar place a lake. There is no exact size rule.
quest.example: A duck pond in a neighborhood park.
quest.note: Ponds are often smaller than lakes, but the names can overlap.

clues: I am a stretch of river where the water rushes and tumbles.
Rocks or a steep riverbed can make my water rough.
Unlike a waterfall, I do not need one clear drop over an edge.
quest.example: Whitewater rapids tumble over rocks in rivers.

clues: I am a raised strip or mound beneath or near the water's surface.
I can be made of rock, coral, or other material.
Coral reefs are home to many sea creatures, but not every one of me is made of coral.
quest.example: Colorful coral reefs grow in warm tropical seas.

clues: I am a natural flow of water traveling through a channel.
The Nile and Amazon are famous examples.
I may flow into another river, a lake, or the sea.
quest.example: The Mississippi River winds across the United States.

clues: I am the place where a river flows into another body of water.
The river might enter a lake, another river, or the sea.
A delta sometimes forms near me, but not every river has one.
quest.example: The Mississippi River empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

clues: I am the place where a river begins.
My water might come from a spring, lake, glacier, or small streams.
I am the starting place, not the direction called upstream.
quest.example: A mountain spring may be a river's source.

clues: I am a large area of salty water, often near land.
Many of me connect to an ocean, and land partly surrounds some of us.
The Mediterranean is a famous example. My name does not follow one strict size or connection rule.
quest.example: The Mediterranean Sea lies between Europe and Africa.

clues: I am the land right beside water.
I can be next to a river, lake, or ocean.
I am the area beside the water; the shoreline is its edge.
quest.example: The shore of a lake is where its water meets land.

clues: I am the edge where land meets water.
My position can move when tides rise or water levels change.
I mark a boundary, not the whole strip of nearby land.
quest.example: A lake's shoreline curves around its edges.

clues: I am water flowing naturally in a channel.
A brook, creek, or river can all be called one of me.
My name does not mean the water must be one particular size.
quest.example: A small stream runs through a wooded park.
quest.note: Brook, creek, river, and stream can describe flowing water. The names often overlap.

clues: I am a stream or river that flows into another stream or river.
I can be large or small.
My water joins the other waterway rather than flowing away from it.
quest.example: The Missouri River joins the Mississippi River.
quest.note: A tributary may be a stream or a river. Its special feature is flowing into another waterway.

clues: I am the direction toward a river's beginning.
A canoe going against the river's flow travels my way.
I lead toward the headwaters, not toward the river's mouth.
quest.example: A canoe going upstream travels toward a river's start.

clues: I happen where flowing water falls over a steep edge.
Water drops from a higher place to a lower one.
Unlike rapids, I have a clear drop or series of drops.
quest.example: Niagara Falls pours over a steep drop.

clues: I am water turning around in a circle.
Currents meeting rocks or other obstacles can help form me.
I am swirling water, not a machine that moves boats.
quest.example: Water can spin in a whirlpool near rocks.

clues: I am a deep valley with steep sides.
A river may cut through rock to form me.
The Grand Canyon is an example. The word gorge can describe similar land.
quest.example: The Grand Canyon has deep sides carved by a river.
quest.note: Canyon and gorge can describe similar steep-sided valleys. There is no exact width rule.

clues: I am a natural hollow or passage in rock.
Water can slowly dissolve some rock, and flowing lava can leave other kinds.
I may go underground, but not every one of me is fully underground.
quest.example: Mammoth Cave has underground passages.

clues: I am a very steep face of rock or earth.
I can stand beside an ocean, valley, or high flat area.
A bluff can also be a steep face; people sometimes use both names.
quest.example: The Cliffs of Moher rise above the ocean in Ireland.
quest.note: Bluff and cliff can describe the same steep face of land.

clues: I am a bowl-shaped hollow in the ground.
A meteorite striking Earth or a volcano can form me.
Some volcanoes have one of me near the top.
quest.example: A volcano may have a bowl-shaped crater at its top.

clues: I am a hill or ridge made mainly of sand.
Wind piles my sand up and changes my shape.
You can find me in deserts and along some beaches.
quest.example: Sand dunes rise in Colorado's Great Sand Dunes.

clues: I am a huge mass of ice on land that moves very slowly.
I form when snow builds up and gets pressed into ice.
I move over land; an iceberg is a piece of ice floating in water.
quest.example: A glacier slowly moves down an Alaskan valley.

clues: I am raised land, often smaller or less steep than a mountain.
My top may be rounded, but not always.
People do not use one worldwide height rule to tell me apart from a mountain.
quest.example: A rounded grassy hill in a park.

clues: I am a large piece of ice floating in the water.
I can break away from a glacier or an ice shelf.
Most of my ice is usually hidden below the water.
quest.example: Icebergs float in the cold North Atlantic Ocean.

clues: I am the solid part of Earth's surface, rather than a body of water.
I can include soil, rocks, plains, and mountains.
I am a broad word for the ground, not just one kind of field or wetland.
quest.example: A grassy farm is one part of Earth's land.

clues: I rise high above the land around me.
I may have steep sides, ridges, and a summit.
The Himalayas have many of me. There is no worldwide height rule separating me from a hill.
quest.example: Mount Everest rises high in the Himalayas.

clues: I am many connected or nearby mountains.
I may contain several high peaks and valleys.
The Andes and Rocky Mountains are examples of me.
quest.example: The Rocky Mountains are a mountain range.

clues: I am a place with water in an otherwise dry area.
Plants and people may be able to live near my water.
I am a watered spot within a dry region, not the whole desert.
quest.example: An oasis may have palms and a pool in a desert.

clues: I am a high point on a mountain or ridge.
I am often pointed, but my shape can vary.
A mountain may have several of me. One may also be its summit.
quest.example: A pointed mountain peak sticks up into the clouds.
quest.note: Peak and summit may mean the same high place. Neither needs a particular height.

clues: I cover a wide area of fairly level land.
I may be flat or gently rolling, without many steep hills.
I do not have to be near sea level. The Great Plains are an example.
quest.example: The Great Plains spread across central North America.

clues: I am a broad area of high land with a fairly level top.
My surface rises above some land around it.
I may look like a huge, flat-topped highland; a mesa is often smaller and more separate.
quest.example: The Colorado Plateau is a broad high land area.
quest.note: Mesas often stand apart, while plateaus cover wider areas. There is no exact size cutoff.

clues: I am a long, raised line of land.
I may run between several mountain tops.
The ground usually slopes down on both sides of my narrow high crest.
quest.example: A ridge can run along the top of a mountain.

clues: I tell how much the ground tilts up or down.
I can be gentle, like a grassy hill, or steep, like a mountainside.
I describe slanting ground, not a separate mountain.
quest.example: Skiers travel downhill on a snowy slope.

clues: I am the highest point of a mountain or another high place.
Climbers may try to reach me.
I can be pointed or rounded; the word peak sometimes means the same thing.
quest.example: A climber might stand on Mount Everest's summit.
quest.note: Peak and summit can mean the same high point, whether it is rounded or pointed.

clues: I am low land between higher hills or mountains.
A river may run through me, or moving ice may have shaped me.
I am the lower area between higher sides, not the top of a mountain.
quest.example: Yosemite Valley sits between high rocky walls.

clues: I have an opening through which melted rock may reach Earth's surface.
During an eruption, I may release lava, ash, and gases.
I do not always look like a cone, and not every mountain is one of me.
quest.example: Mount St. Helens in Washington is a volcano.

clues: I am a place that gets very little rain or snow.
I can be hot or cold; parts of Antarctica are examples.
Being very dry defines me, not always having sand or cacti.
quest.example: The Sahara Desert receives very little rainfall.

clues: I am an open area of land.
People may grow crops on me or use me for sports.
I describe an open place or how it is used, not how high the land is.
quest.example: A grassy field where children play soccer.

clues: I am a large area where trees are the main plants.
Animals, mushrooms, and smaller plants can live among my trees.
People may also use the words woods or woodland for similar places.
quest.example: The Amazon Rainforest has millions of trees.
quest.note: Forest, woods, and woodland can describe similar tree-filled areas.

clues: I am a wet place where grasses and reeds are the main plants.
Water may cover my ground for part or all of the year.
Unlike many swamps, I usually do not have many trees growing through me.
quest.example: Grassy marshes grow in the Florida Everglades.

clues: I am open land covered mostly with grass and other low plants.
Wildflowers may grow here, and people may mow or graze animals here.
I can also be called a kind of field; the words can overlap.
quest.example: A meadow covered in grass and wildflowers.

clues: I am something found in nature that people can use.
Fresh water, wood, rocks, and sunlight are examples.
I can be a material or a source of energy.
quest.example: Freshwater, trees, and stone can be useful resources.

clues: I am the mixture of tiny rock pieces, decayed material, air, and water near the ground's surface.
Plants grow roots through me, and small living things help make me.
I am more specific than the word land.
quest.example: Roots grow down into dark, crumbly soil.

clues: I am a wet area where trees or shrubs grow.
Water may stand or move slowly around my plants.
Unlike a marsh, I usually have many woody plants.
quest.example: Cypress trees can grow in a flooded swamp.

clues: I am all the plants growing in an area.
Grasses, bushes, and trees are parts of me.
I mean the plant cover, not the soil beneath it.
quest.example: Grass, bushes, and trees are all vegetation.

clues: I am an area with many trees.
People sometimes use my name for a smaller forest.
There is no exact size rule separating me from a forest.
quest.example: A small patch of woods behind a house.
quest.note: Woods, woodland, and forest are names that can overlap.

clues: I am a waterway that people build or greatly change.
Boats may travel through me, or I may carry water to fields.
The Panama Canal is a famous example.
quest.example: Ships travel through the Panama Canal.

clues: I am a place with land, borders, and a government.
Japan and Brazil are examples.
I am a political place, not a natural land shape.
quest.example: Brazil is a country in South America.

clues: I am a wall or barrier built across a river or stream.
I may hold back water and create a reservoir.
I usually cross the waterway; a levee usually runs beside it.
quest.example: Hoover Dam holds back water in a river.

clues: I am a platform built out over water from the land.
Posts or other supports often hold me up.
People fish or tie up boats on me. Some places use the word wharf for a similar structure.
quest.example: A fishing pier reaches out over the ocean.
quest.note: Pier and wharf can describe similar structures beside water.

clues: I am a passage through or under something.
People build me for cars, trains, or water, though some occur naturally.
I let something travel through a mountain or under an obstacle.
quest.example: A road tunnel can pass straight through a mountain.

clues: Africa and Antarctica are examples of me.
I am one of Earth's very large land divisions.
Many schools teach seven of me, but other ways of grouping them exist.
quest.example: South America is one of Earth's continents.

clues: I am the planet where we live.
I have oceans and continents on my surface.
I travel around the Sun and have one natural moon.
quest.example: Earth is the planet where we live.

clues: I am the line where the sky seems to meet land or water.
What you see of me depends on where you stand.
I am an edge you see in the distance, not a real line on the ground.
quest.example: At sea, the distant water seems to touch the sky.

clues: I am a group or chain of islands.
My islands can form in different ways, including from volcanoes or coral.
Indonesia is an example of me.
quest.example: Indonesia is an archipelago of many islands.

clues: I am a ring-shaped coral reef or group of coral islands.
A shallow area of water, called a lagoon, lies inside my ring.
Many form as coral grows around an island that slowly sinks.
quest.example: Some Maldives islands form rings around lagoons.

clues: I am a slow-moving waterway often found in low, wet places.
Many of me are found in Louisiana.
My regional name can describe a creek, channel, or waterway through wetlands.
quest.example: Slow, winding bayous run through Louisiana.
quest.note: Bayou is a regional word for a slow-flowing waterway, often in wet lowlands.

clues: I am a small stream or a fork of a larger waterway.
I can join other flowing channels.
In some places, my name means much the same as stream or tributary.
quest.example: A small branch of a river joins the main flow.
quest.note: Branch, tributary, and stream can name similar waterways in some places.

clues: I am waves that tip forward and crash.
My tops tumble into white foam, often near shore.
I am the waves as they break, not all the water in the ocean.
quest.example: Breaking waves crash into white foam near beaches.

clues: I am a route or passage for moving water or boats.
I may be natural or changed by people.
A canal is a human-built kind of me.
quest.example: Ships follow deep channels through shallow waters.

clues: I am part of a continent that continues underwater.
I am often fairly shallow near the coast.
I stretch out toward deeper water, where the sea floor slopes down more sharply.
quest.example: The continental shelf lies under shallow sea near shore.

clues: I am the land area where rainwater drains toward the same river or outlet.
Streams in this area may join one another.
People also call me a watershed in many places.
quest.example: Rain over a drainage basin flows to one river.
quest.note: Watershed and drainage basin usually name the same area of land.

clues: I am coastal water where a river meets the sea.
Fresh river water and salty sea water often mix in me.
Chesapeake Bay is an example. Not every part of me has the same amount of salt.
quest.example: Chesapeake Bay is an estuary where fresh and salt water mix.

clues: I am a long, narrow arm of the sea between steep slopes.
A glacier carved the valley now filled with seawater.
Norway has many famous examples of me.
quest.example: Norway has fjords cut by ancient glaciers.

clues: I am low, fairly flat land beside a river.
River water may spread over me during a flood.
Over time, floodwater can leave new layers of sand or mud here.
quest.example: When a river overtops its banks, water spreads across the low ground beside it.

clues: I am coastal land that sticks out beyond the nearby shore.
I may have high or steep sides.
People may also call a place like me a cape.
quest.example: A rocky headland reaches out beyond a coast.
quest.note: Cape and headland can describe the same coastal land that sticks out into water.

clues: I am a narrow arm or opening of water reaching into land.
I may connect a larger body of water to a smaller one.
Some bays and coves may also be called by my name.
quest.example: A narrow inlet lets sea water reach into land.
quest.note: Some inlets are also called bays or coves. The names can overlap.

clues: I am shallow water set apart from a larger sea by sand or coral.
A sandbar or reef may form a barrier, sometimes with gaps.
I often sit behind that barrier near the coast.
quest.example: A shallow lagoon may sit behind a coral reef.

clues: I am a big bend in a river or stream.
Water may wear away the outside of my curve and leave sand on the inside.
Several of my bends can make a river look winding.
quest.example: A river curves through its floodplain in a series of sweeping bends.

clues: I am a curved lake left beside a river.
I may form when the river takes a shorter route and cuts off one of its bends.
My shape often looks like a horseshoe.
quest.example: A river cuts across a bend, leaving a curved lake beside its newer, straighter channel.

clues: I am a raised strip or pile of sand in water.
Waves or currents can move sand and build me up.
I may be underwater or above the surface as water levels change.
quest.example: A sandbar may form near a river mouth.

clues: I am a place where underground water comes out naturally.
My water may begin a stream or fill a pool.
I am where groundwater reaches the surface.
quest.example: Groundwater emerges on a hillside and feeds a small stream.

clues: I am a narrow passage of water.
I connect two larger bodies of water, with land on both sides.
The Strait of Gibraltar is an example. An isthmus is narrow land instead.
quest.example: The Strait of Gibraltar is narrow water between lands.

clues: I am the regular rise and fall of sea level.
The Moon's and Sun's gravity are the main causes of me.
I may be high or low at different times along the shore.
quest.example: High tide lifts the water higher along a beach.

clues: I am land where rainwater and streams drain toward the same place.
I am often another name for a drainage basin.
Sometimes people use my name for the high land that separates two drainage areas.
quest.example: Rain in a watershed drains toward the same water system.
quest.note: Watershed often means drainage basin. In some places it means the ridge separating drainage areas.

clues: I am a low area of land with higher ground around it.
Some examples collect water, while others stay dry.
My shape is like a shallow bowl, but not every one drains to a single river.
quest.example: A low basin can collect rainwater after a storm.

clues: I am a steep bank or wall of land above lower ground or water.
A river may wear away land and leave one of me.
People sometimes use the word cliff for a similar steep face.
quest.example: Some tall bluffs overlook the Mississippi River.
quest.note: Bluff and cliff can describe similar steep land.

clues: I am a deep gap or opening with steep sides.
Rock can crack, or water can wear the land away to make me.
Some canyons and gorges may also be described by my name.
quest.example: A deep chasm splits rock with steep sides.
quest.note: Chasm, canyon, and gorge can describe similar deep gaps with steep sides.

clues: I am a small, often steep-sided type of volcano.
Loose pieces of erupted rock pile up around an opening.
My cone is made mostly of these volcanic pieces, called cinders.
quest.example: A cinder cone volcano is built from small rock pieces.

clues: I am a deep, narrow valley with steep sides.
Running water may carve me into rock.
People sometimes call a similar place a canyon.
quest.example: A river may run through a steep rocky gorge.
quest.note: Gorge and canyon can describe similar steep-sided valleys.

clues: I am a high landform with a broad, flat top and steep sides.
I often stand apart from nearby high land.
My name comes from the Spanish word for table.
quest.example: A mesa looks like a table standing in a desert.
quest.note: A mesa often stands apart and looks like a table. A plateau is usually a wider high area.

clues: I am a pile or ridge of rocks and soil left by moving ice.
A glacier may carry these pieces and leave them behind.
I form through glacier movement, not from sand piled up by wind.
quest.example: A ridge of mixed stones and sediment remains along the margin of a retreating glacier.
quest.note: A moraine contains rock and soil moved or left by a glacier, not just sand blown by wind.

clues: I am a wetland where partly decayed plants build up over time.
Rain is often my main source of water.
Mosses, including sphagnum moss, often grow in my wet, acidic soil.
quest.example: A bog can feel spongy because of wet moss.

clues: I am a grassy ecosystem especially common in North America.
Many grasses grow here, with few trees in open areas.
I am more than a small lawn or field; I am a large natural grassland.
quest.example: Tall grasses wave across the North American prairie.

clues: I am a very cold region where tall trees are rare or absent.
Plants such as mosses, grasses, and small shrubs can grow here.
I have a short growing season. Some areas have permanently frozen ground.
quest.example: Arctic tundra has few trees and short summers.
quest.note: Tundra can be near the Arctic or high on mountains. Frozen ground is common in Arctic tundra, but not everywhere.

clues: I am land where water stays in or near the soil for long periods.
Water shapes what kinds of soil and plants I have.
Marshes, swamps, and bogs are examples of me.
quest.example: Waterlogged ground supports plants adapted to saturated soil.

clues: I am a raised bank beside a river that can help limit flooding.
I run along the river rather than across its channel.
People can build me, but rivers can also leave raised banks naturally.
quest.example: A levee beside a river helps block floodwater.

clues: I am a water-filled chamber with gates that boats can enter.
Water rises or falls inside me to lift or lower the boat.
I help boats move between different water levels in canals or rivers.
quest.example: Canal locks raise and lower boats using gates.

clues: I am a place where water is stored for later use.
My water may supply homes, farms, or power stations.
A dam can help form me, but not all examples are behind dams.
quest.example: Lake Mead is a reservoir that stores water.

clues: I am a waterside structure where ships can stop.
People may load cargo, unload it, or tie up boats here.
I am often built along the shore; the word pier sometimes overlaps.
quest.example: Ships load and unload cargo at a wharf.
quest.note: Pier and wharf sometimes mean the same kind of waterside structure.

clues: I tell how high something is compared with a chosen starting level.
A plane's height above sea level is one example.
People also use the word elevation for height in similar situations.
quest.example: A plane might fly at an altitude of 10,000 feet.
quest.note: Altitude and elevation both describe height. Altitude is often used for planes.

clues: I am a symbol on a map that shows directions.
I may show north, south, east, and west around a center.
I help you find your direction, not measure how far away a place is.
quest.example: A compass rose on a park map helps a walker identify north, south, east and west.

clues: I am a line on a map joining places at the same height.
Groups of me show the shapes of hills and valleys.
When my lines are close together, the ground is usually steep.
quest.example: A contour labeled 100 meters joins map positions at that elevation.

clues: I am numbers or values that tell where a place is.
A pair of latitude and longitude numbers is one example.
Different maps can use different sets of numbers to find a position.
quest.example: A map location can be specified with a latitude such as 20°N and a longitude such as 10°E.

clues: I tell how high a place is compared with sea level or another starting level.
A map may use me to show how high the ground is.
Altitude can mean something similar; the words can overlap.
quest.example: Denver is about 5,280 feet above sea level.
quest.note: Altitude and elevation both describe height. Elevation is often used for places on land.

clues: I am an imaginary line halfway between Earth's North and South Poles.
My latitude is zero degrees.
I divide Earth into northern and southern halves.
quest.example: On a classroom globe, zero degrees latitude circles the middle between the poles.

clues: I am one half of a round ball or sphere.
Earth has a Northern and Southern one.
You can also divide Earth into eastern and western halves.
quest.example: The equator divides a globe into northern and southern halves.

clues: I tell how far north or south a place is from the equator.
I am measured in degrees, from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles.
Lines of equal north-or-south position circle Earth.
quest.example: A point at 20°N is north of the equator; a point at 20°S is south of it.

clues: I tell how far east or west a place is from a starting line called the prime meridian.
My lines run from one pole to the other.
I work with latitude to help show a place's position.
quest.example: Two locations at 10°E lie on the same meridian, even if one is farther north.

clues: I explain the symbols and colors on a map.
I might tell you that a blue line means a river.
I am also called a map legend.
quest.example: A map key might explain that a dotted line marks a walking path and a blue patch marks water.

clues: I help you compare map distances with real distances.
I may look like a marked bar or a written rule.
For example, 1 centimeter on a map may stand for 1 kilometer on Earth.
quest.example: If a map uses 1 centimeter for 1 kilometer, a 3-centimeter route represents 3 kilometers.

clues: I am the place where Earth's spinning axis meets the far northern surface.
My latitude is 90° north.
I am the geographic point, which is different from the moving magnetic north pole.
quest.example: The northern end of Earth’s rotation axis meets the surface at the North Pole.

clues: I am the place where Earth's spinning axis meets the far southern surface.
My latitude is 90° south.
I am on Antarctica, unlike the North Pole in the Arctic Ocean.
quest.example: The southern end of Earth’s rotation axis meets the surface at the South Pole.

clues: I am a map that shows the shape and height of the land.
I often use contour lines to show hills and valleys.
Walkers can use me to spot steep hills, ridges, and low valleys.
quest.example: A walker uses contour patterns on a topographic map to spot a steep hillside.

clues: I am rock or loose material underground that can hold and pass along water.
Water fills tiny spaces or cracks inside me.
A well may draw water from me; I am not usually an underground lake.
quest.example: A well draws groundwater from water-filled pores in sand or cracks in rock.

clues: I happen when moving water, wind, or ice drops material it was carrying.
A slowing river may leave sand behind.
I build up piles or layers of sediment instead of carrying them away.
quest.example: A river slows and leaves a sandbar beside its channel.

clues: I happen when water, wind, ice, or gravity moves earth materials.
I may carry soil, sand, or rock fragments to another place.
Weathering breaks rock down; I move the loosened material away.
quest.example: After rain, a stream carries loosened sand downstream.

clues: I am a kind of hot spring that sometimes shoots water and steam into the air.
Heat and pressure build up in underground passages.
Old Faithful is a famous example of me.
quest.example: Hot water erupts periodically from a vent at the ground’s surface.
quest.note: A geyser is a special kind of hot spring that sometimes shoots out water and steam.

clues: I am a spring where water is warmed by heat inside Earth.
Warm groundwater comes out at the surface.
Unlike a geyser, I do not have to shoot water into the air.
quest.example: Groundwater heated below the surface emerges in a warm pool.
quest.note: A geyser is a kind of hot spring that erupts. Other hot springs do not need to erupt.

clues: I happen when rock breaks apart or changes without being carried away.
Water freezing in cracks, chemicals, and living things can help cause me.
Erosion moves material elsewhere; I change it where it is.
quest.example: Water freezes inside a rock crack and helps widen it without transporting the rock away.

compare.explanation: Both are bodies of water surrounded by land. Ponds are often smaller or shallower than lakes, but there is no worldwide rule for the names.
compare.example: Lake Michigan is a very large lake. A duck pond in a neighborhood park.

compare.explanation: An island has water on every side. A peninsula has water on most sides but stays connected to other land.
compare.example: Hawaii has many islands surrounded by ocean. Florida sticks out into the Atlantic and Gulf waters.

compare.explanation: A stream is flowing water in a channel. A river is one kind of stream. Creek and brook can mean similar things, so the names overlap.
compare.example: The Mississippi River winds across the United States. A small stream runs through a wooded park.

compare.explanation: Both rise above nearby land. Mountains are often higher or steeper than hills, but there is no worldwide height rule.
compare.example: Mount Everest rises high in the Himalayas. A rounded grassy hill in a park.

compare.explanation: A valley is low land between higher places. A canyon is a valley with steep sides. The same place may be both; gorge is another similar word.
compare.example: Yosemite Valley sits between high rocky walls. The Grand Canyon has deep sides carved by a river.

compare.explanation: A forest has trees as its main plants. A meadow is open land covered mostly in grasses and other low plants.
compare.example: The Amazon Rainforest has millions of trees. A meadow covered in grass and wildflowers.

compare.explanation: Oceans are huge, connected bodies of salty water. Lakes are surrounded by land. Some lakes are salty, so salt alone does not tell them apart.
compare.example: The Pacific Ocean covers a huge part of Earth. Lake Michigan is a very large lake.

compare.explanation: A beach is loose sand, shells, or stones beside water. A cliff is a steep rock or earth face. You can find a beach below a cliff.
compare.example: A sandy Atlantic Ocean beach in Florida. The Cliffs of Moher rise above the ocean in Ireland.

compare.explanation: A waterfall has a clear drop in flowing water. Rapids are fast, rough stretches of a river. Both may happen on the same river.
compare.example: Niagara Falls pours over a steep drop. Whitewater rapids tumble over rocks in rivers.

compare.explanation: Both have wet ground. Swamps usually have many trees or shrubs. Marshes have mostly grasses and reeds.
compare.example: Cypress trees can grow in a flooded swamp. Grassy marshes grow in the Florida Everglades.

compare.explanation: A desert gets very little rain or snow. An oasis is a place with water in an otherwise dry area.
compare.example: The Sahara Desert receives very little rainfall. An oasis may have palms and a pool in a desert.

compare.explanation: A river's source is where it starts. Its mouth is where it enters a lake, another river, or the sea.
compare.example: A mountain spring may be a river's source. The Mississippi River empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

compare.explanation: Upstream means toward the river's beginning, against the flow. Downstream means in the same direction the river flows.
compare.example: A canoe going upstream travels toward a river's start. A floating leaf goes downstream with the current.

compare.explanation: The shore is the land beside water. The shoreline is the edge where water meets land. That edge may move as water levels change.
compare.example: The shore of a lake is where its water meets land. A lake's shoreline curves around its edges.

compare.explanation: A summit is the highest point of a mountain. A valley is low land between higher hills or mountains.
compare.example: A climber might stand on Mount Everest's summit. Yosemite Valley sits between high rocky walls.

compare.explanation: A cave is a natural opening in rock large enough to enter. A tunnel is a passage through or beneath something. Many tunnels are built, but some are natural.
compare.example: Mammoth Cave has underground passages. A road tunnel can pass straight through a mountain.

compare.explanation: A hill is raised ground that may be made of rock, soil, or other material. A dune is a mound or ridge made mainly of wind-blown sand.
compare.example: A rounded grassy hill in a park. Sand dunes rise in Colorado's Great Sand Dunes.

compare.explanation: A glacier is a large mass of ice that slowly moves on land. An iceberg is a piece of ice that has broken away and floats in water.
compare.example: A glacier slowly moves down an Alaskan valley. Icebergs float in the cold North Atlantic Ocean.

compare.explanation: Both names describe coastal water partly surrounded by land. A gulf is often large, but there is no exact size rule separating gulfs and bays.
compare.example: San Francisco Bay curves into the land. The Gulf of Mexico is partly surrounded by land.

compare.explanation: A pier is a platform built out over water. A harbor is a sheltered area of water where boats can stay.
compare.example: A fishing pier reaches out over the ocean. New York Harbor provides sheltered water for ships.

compare.explanation: Woods are areas with many trees. A field is open land used for growing plants, playing sports, or other activities.
compare.example: A small patch of woods behind a house. A grassy field where children play soccer.

compare.explanation: Both can be fairly flat. A plateau is high land with a broad, fairly level top. A plain does not have to be high.
compare.example: The Great Plains spread across central North America. The Colorado Plateau is a broad high land area.

compare.explanation: A summit is the highest point of a mountain or other high place. A peak is often a pointed high place. The same spot can be both.
compare.example: A pointed mountain peak sticks up into the clouds. A climber might stand on Mount Everest's summit.

compare.explanation: Coast usually means land beside an ocean or sea. Shore can also mean land beside a lake or river. Their meanings overlap at the ocean.
compare.example: Florida's Atlantic coast is next to the ocean. The shore of a lake is where its water meets land.

compare.explanation: A current is water flowing in a direction. A wave is a disturbance traveling through water; water moves as the wave passes, too.
compare.example: An ocean current carries water along the coast. Ocean waves roll toward a beach and rise and fall.

compare.explanation: A volcano has an opening where melted rock may rise and erupt. A mountain is raised land. Some volcanoes are mountains, but many mountains are not volcanoes.
compare.example: Mount St. Helens in Washington is a volcano. Mount Everest rises high in the Himalayas.

compare.explanation: A river is a flowing waterway. A tributary is a waterway that flows into another one. A river can also be a tributary.
compare.example: The Mississippi River winds across the United States. The Missouri River joins the Mississippi River.

compare.explanation: A beach is loose sand or stones along a shore. A sandbar is a buildup of sand in or across water. Changing water levels can connect them.
compare.example: A sandbar may form near a river mouth. A sandy Atlantic Ocean beach in Florida.

compare.explanation: A dam is a barrier that holds back or controls water. A reservoir is a place where water is stored. Many reservoirs form behind dams.
compare.example: Hoover Dam holds back water in a river. Lake Mead is a reservoir that stores water.

compare.explanation: A river mouth is where a river enters another body of water. A delta is land built from sand and mud the river leaves near some mouths.
compare.example: The Mississippi River makes a delta near the Gulf. The Mississippi River empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

compare.explanation: An estuary is coastal water where river water and seawater often mix. A delta is sediment built up near a river mouth. One place can have both.
compare.example: Chesapeake Bay is an estuary where fresh and salt water mix. The Mississippi River makes a delta near the Gulf.

compare.explanation: An archipelago is a group of islands. An atoll is a ring of coral reef or coral islands around a lagoon. Some atolls include several islands.
compare.example: Some Maldives islands form rings around lagoons. Indonesia is an archipelago of many islands.

compare.explanation: A strait is a narrow strip of water connecting larger bodies of water. An isthmus is a narrow strip of land joining larger land areas.
compare.example: The Strait of Gibraltar is narrow water between lands. The Isthmus of Panama links two larger land areas.

compare.explanation: A bluff is often a steep bank above land or water. A cliff is a steep face of rock or earth. Both names may describe the same place.
compare.example: Some tall bluffs overlook the Mississippi River. The Cliffs of Moher rise above the ocean in Ireland.

compare.explanation: A fjord is a long, narrow sea inlet carved by a glacier. A cove is a smaller, sheltered bay. Both can be along a coast.
compare.example: Norway has fjords cut by ancient glaciers. A small sheltered cove might hold tiny boats.

compare.explanation: A levee runs beside a river to help keep floodwater in its channel. A dam crosses a waterway and holds back or controls water.
compare.example: A levee beside a river helps block floodwater. Hoover Dam holds back water in a river.

compare.explanation: A watershed is land where rainwater drains toward the same river or outlet. A river is the flowing water in a channel. A watershed can contain many rivers.
compare.example: Rain in a watershed drains toward the same water system. The Mississippi River winds across the United States.

compare.explanation: Both tell how high something is compared with a starting level. Elevation is often used for the ground and altitude for aircraft, but the words overlap.
compare.example: Denver is about 5,280 feet above sea level. A plane might fly at an altitude of 10,000 feet.

compare.explanation: Both are high areas with fairly flat tops. A mesa is often a separate, table-shaped landform. A plateau usually covers a wider area, but there is no exact size cutoff.
compare.example: A mesa looks like a table standing in a desert. The Colorado Plateau is a broad high land area.

compare.explanation: A channel is a route where water flows or boats travel. A canal is a waterway people build or greatly change. A canal is one kind of channel.
compare.example: Ships travel through the Panama Canal. Ships follow deep channels through shallow waters.

compare.explanation: Latitude tells how far north or south a place is from the equator. Longitude tells how far east or west it is from a starting line. Together they locate places.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Weathering breaks down or changes rock where it is. Erosion moves soil and rock pieces to new places. Weathered pieces can later be carried away.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Erosion carries soil, sand, or rock pieces away. Deposition happens when that moving material is dropped somewhere else.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: An aquifer is rock or loose material underground that stores and passes along water. A spring is a place where groundwater naturally comes out at the surface.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Both have water heated inside Earth. A geyser is a special hot spring that sometimes shoots hot water and steam into the air.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A river is flowing water in a channel. A floodplain is the low land beside it that can be covered with water during a flood.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A meander is a bend in a flowing river. An oxbow lake can form when a river changes course and leaves an old bend cut off.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A map scale tells how a distance on the map compares with real distance. A map key explains what the map's colors and symbols mean.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A contour line joins places that are the same height. A line of longitude joins places with the same east-or-west position.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: The North and South Poles are opposite ends of Earth's spinning axis at the surface. These geographic poles differ from magnetic poles.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A glacier is a large mass of ice slowly moving over land. A moraine is a pile or ridge of stones and soil a glacier carries or leaves behind.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Wetland is the broad name for land where water shapes the soil and living things. A marsh is one type of wetland, usually full of grasses or reeds.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: The equator is an imaginary line at 0° latitude around Earth. A hemisphere is half a sphere. The equator divides Earth into northern and southern halves.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A river's source is where it begins. A spring is where underground water comes out naturally. Some rivers begin at springs, but not all do.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A dune is a mound of sand shaped mainly by wind. A moraine is a pile or ridge of rocks and soil moved or left by a glacier.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.
